To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the absolute proper motions in both the U- and V-components of a large sample of stars toward the south Galactic polar cap are well represented by a model having a large LSR rotational speed of 270 ± 20 km s-1.
the LSR is moving at a speed of 270 ± 30 km s-1 and the solar peculiar motion is (11, 5, 7) km s-1.
the Sun is moving with respect to the Local Standard of Rest at 270 ± 10 km s-1 and that the Milky Way has a mass of 1.2 ×1012 M☭ to 50 kpc.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the absolute proper motion of the Sun, the LSR velocity, and the mass of the Milky Way, and it provides a consistent picture of the Galaxy and its environment.
the absolute proper motion of the Galaxy and with the determination of the mass of our Galaxy.

the following issues: (1) the absolute nature of the LSR speed, (2) the absolute proper motions in U and V, (3) the mass of the Galactic dark halo, and (4) the mass of M31 and its implications for the formation and evolution of the Milky Way-M31 pair.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mass of the Milky Way is in the range 1-2 × 1013 M☉.
the mass of the Milky Way is between ~1 and ~5 × 1012 solar masses within 50 kpc.
the Galaxy has a large mass, but that the mass is not as large as the mass inferred from the rotation curve.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have measured, for the first time, the absolute rotational speed of the Galaxy and found it to be 270 km s1, which is consistent with the gravitational mass inferred from the motion and distance of the LMC and with the mass inferred from the timing argument.

the Milky Way mass inferred from the motion and the orbital period of the LMC is not in contradiction with the mass inferred from the rotation of the Galaxy and that the LMC is a good tracer of the Galactic mass.

our derived LSR speed is consistent with the mass of our Galaxy inferred from the proper motion of M31, the timing argument, and the Clouds, and that our derived solar peculiar motion is consistent with a Galactic disk that is not expanding or contracting locally.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mass of the Milky Way is larger than previously thought, with the implication that the mass of M31 must also be increased.
the LSR speed of the Milky Way is large enough to allow the Galaxy to be a massive system with a large halo.
a large LSR is not necessarily in conflict with the mass of our Galaxy.
